claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength in its simple solid-solution state.
The low hardness and strength are governed primarily by a nearly ideal random chemical configuration with minimal short-range order.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy lacks nanoscale chemical clustering or ordering.
Absence of nanoscale ordering or clustering lowers the critical stress for dislocation glide.
Lower resistance to dislocation glide enhances plasticity and machinability while reducing hardness and strength.
The initial material is a single-phase, chemically random CoCrFeNiTi solid solution with minimal SRO and nanoscale precipitates.
A controlled heat treatment can promote measurable SRO in CoCrFeNiTi without changing its overall crystal structure.
A minor alloying treatment can promote SRO or nanoscale precipitation without changing the overall crystal structure.
SRO can act as a pinning obstacle to dislocation motion.
Nanoscale precipitates can act as pinning centers that hinder dislocation motion.
A uniform elemental distribution in disordered CoCrFeNiTi produces low lattice friction and relatively unimpeded dislocation glide.
Chemical ordering creates energy barriers that impede dislocation motion.
SRO or nanoscale precipitates create local stress fields that impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion from induced ordering or precipitation will increase hardness and compressive strength.
The strengthening caused by induced SRO or nanoscale precipitation will reduce plastic strain.
Relative to the starting alloy, treated CoCrFeNiTi will have significantly higher hardness and compressive strength and lower plastic strain.
Nanoscale deformation behavior can depend on alloy chemistry, crystal structure, thermomechanical processing, and deformation state.
Grain size, processing defects, and residual stresses may interact with or mask an SRO contribution to mechanical behavior.
The proposed comparison is limited to approximately 25–600 °C under quasi-static loading.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant hardness and compressive-strength increase, or failure to obtain the predicted plasticity decrease, is designated as falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention permits a minor alloying addition, but the controlled comparison and boundary describe both samples as equimolar CoCrFeNiTi. An added alloying element or unequal substitution would no longer be the same equimolar composition unless explicitly balanced.

The proposed mediator includes precipitate formation, while the hypothesis is restricted to a maintained single-phase solid solution. Genuine precipitates normally constitute a second phase, so precipitation is inconsistent with the single-phase boundary unless only SRO within one phase is used.
